items.abstract: <jats:p>Wood technology likely played a key role in human evolution, yet it remains poorly documented because organic materials rarely preserve in archaeological contexts. The Middle Palaeolithic site of Abric Romaní (Capellades, Barcelona) provides exceptional evidence of Neanderthal woodworking preserved through travertine incrustation. We document 597 wooden imprints and charred wood remains recovered from 16 archaeological levels dated between ∼62,000 and 40,000 years ago. The assemblage includes wood imprints, charred wood imprints, and charred macroremains, among which several anthropogenic objects can be identified. These include tools and weapons, domestic artifacts, and structural elements, revealing a wide range of woodworking activities. Key discoveries include wooden spears, pointed sticks, and domestic objects such as trays and tripods. A club-like artifact recovered from level P represents a unique object with no clear parallel in the prehistoric record. The Abric Romaní assemblage highlights the importance of wood within Neanderthal technological systems and provides previously unknown insights into the role of organic materials in Middle Palaeolithic societies.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Sequence variations in fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 (FGFR2) are associated with craniosynostosis syndromes, disrupting craniofacial development, yet early mandibular alterations remain poorly characterized. This study examined Meckel's cartilage (MC) and mandibular morphology in mouse models of Apert (
                    <jats:italic>Fgfr2</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sup>
                      <jats:italic>+/P253R</jats:italic>
                    </jats:sup>
                    ) and Crouzon (
                    <jats:italic>Fgfr2c</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sup>
                      <jats:italic>C342Y/+</jats:italic>
                    </jats:sup>
                    ) syndromes using Euclidean distance matrix analysis and finite element modeling at embryonic days 14.5 and 16.5. Apert mice exhibited significant MC shortening and elevated, widespread strain in the growth center area correlating with mandibular shortening and asymmetry. In contrast, Crouzon mice showed minor MC changes and localized strain peaks with larger mandibles. These biomechanical perturbations in Meckel's cartilage are associated with distinct mandibular phenotypes, consistent with a bidirectional relationship in which altered strain environments may both influence and reflect mandibular dysmorphogenesis during early development. The findings enhance our understanding of the biomechanical basis of mandibular anomalies associated with FGFR2 mutations, informing future investigations into craniofacial morphogenesis.
                  </jats:p>
authors: Fred R. Foster, Alexandre Freire, Ana Cláudia Rossi, Jordan Wilson, Joan T. Richtsmeier, Kazuhiko Kawasaki, Felippe B. Prado, Susan M. Motch Perrine

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    This preamble honors the late evolutionary primatologists Judith Masters and Fabien Génin, synthesizing their profound impact on strepsirrhine anatomy, systematics, and biogeography. Over four decades, Masters applied Hugh Paterson's Recognition Concept of species alongside comprehensive craniodental morphometrics and phylogenetics to reframe the evolutionary trees of nocturnal African galagos, culminating in the formal description of the dwarf galago genus
                    <jats:italic>Paragalago</jats:italic>
                    . Génin complemented this systematic framework by linking sensory ecology with comparative physiology, providing groundbreaking evidence of energetic plasticity—such as facultative heterothermy and torpor—in Malagasy mouse lemurs. Together, their collaborative research challenged major primatological paradigms by refuting the “primitive” status of cheirogaleids and critiquing standard socio‐ecological models in favor of species‐recognition frameworks driven by sensory drive. Furthermore, their interdisciplinary work proposed an alternative view of vertebrate colonization of Madagascar. Beyond their empirical contributions, they established the African Primate Initiative for Ecology and Speciation (APIES) and the Primate Ecology and Genetics Group (PEGG), leaving a lasting legacy of regional capacity‐building and postgraduate mentorship that reshaped southern African primatology.
                  </jats:p>
authors: Sébastien Couette, Curswan A. Andrews, Luca Pozzi, Trudy Turner, Massimiliano Delpero
